nameStory: The humpbacked orbweaver gets its name from the distinctive rounded hump or bulge on the back part of its abdomen, which gives it a characteristic silhouette that's easy to spot even from a distance. This prominent 'hunchback' appearance makes it stand out among the many orbweaver spiders that might otherwise look quite similar.
description: The humpbacked orbweaver is a medium-sized spider that builds the classic circular webs we often picture when we think of spider webs. What makes this orbweaver special is the noticeable rounded hump on the rear portion of its abdomen, giving it an unmistakable profile. These spiders typically measure about half an inch in body length, with females being noticeably larger than males. Their coloration tends to be mottled browns and grays that help them blend in with tree bark and vegetation.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Look for the telltale rounded hump or bulge on the back end of the abdomen - it feels firm if gently touched and creates a distinctive silhouette that looks almost like the spider is carrying a backpack

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds classic circular orb webs with sticky spiral threads radiating from the center, often positioned vertically between branches with a slightly irregular, handmade appearance

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Abdomen displays mottled patterns of brown, gray, and sometimes yellowish colors that feel slightly fuzzy to the touch and help the spider blend with bark textures

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Females reach about 12-15mm in body length (roughly thumbnail-sized), while males are considerably smaller at around 7-9mm

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits head-down in the center of its web during the day, or hides nearby in a silk retreat that feels papery and is usually attached to a leaf or bark crevice

habitat: Humpbacked orbweavers prefer wooded areas and forest edges throughout New England, where they string their webs between shrubs, small trees, and understory vegetation. You'll often find them in mixed hardwood forests, along woodland trails, and in suburban areas with plenty of trees and bushes. They seem to favor spots that are somewhat sheltered but still get dappled sunlight filtering through the canopy.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing in late spring as temperatures warm, starting to build their first webs of the season in sheltered woodland spots.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, actively maintaining webs and feeding. This is the best time to spot their characteristic humped silhouette in webs.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs and females produce egg sacs before the first frost. Adults remain active until cold weather sets in.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically don't survive freezing temperatures, but egg sacs overwinter attached to protected surfaces like bark crevices or under eaves.

funFact: The hump on this spider's back isn't just for show - it's actually filled with part of their digestive system, essentially making them walking stomachs that can process large meals more efficiently than their flat-backed cousins!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other orbweaver species, but the prominent abdominal hump is a dead giveaway - if you see that distinctive 'backpack' bulge, you've found a humpbacked orbweaver. Remember: 'Hump equals humpbacked' - no other common New England orbweaver has such a pronounced rounded bulge on the rear of the abdomen.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'humpbacked,' this spider's posture is perfectly normal for its species - the hump isn't a deformity or injury but rather its natural body shape that has evolved for specific functional purposes.
compareHints: Since this is the only Eustala species commonly found in New England, compare it with other orbweavers like the cross orbweaver or marbled orbweaver. The key difference is that distinctive abdominal hump - other orbweavers may be round or elongated, but none have that characteristic bulging 'backpack' shape. The humpbacked orbweaver also tends to be less colorful than many of its orbweaver relatives.
